rationale:
What the critique got right: my draft (wheel_track 0.16, kd 1.5, base_speed 1.4, sensor_size 0.016, mass 0.6) was never raced, and its stated baseline was wrong. Its changes were confounded, and kd 1.5 amplifies sensor noise by 100*kd per unit of signal change per step. I reject the draft.

What I kept: the critique's main demand that the next race be attributable to a known baseline. I return to the best raced design, iteration 7 (score 58.1734; oval 63.49, s-bend 66.85, slalom 44.19; no completions). Its values are exactly those raced: sensors at y 0.08 with x from -0.03 to +0.03 at 0.01 m spacing, sensor_size 0.012, wheel_track 0.12, mass 0.8, kp 4.5, ki 0, kd 0.1, base_speed 1.5, linear weights, line_loss 'last_direction'.

Why no change: iteration 8 changed only base_speed (1.5 to 1.3) and scored 58.1734, identical to iteration 7 to four decimals. Speed therefore has no measurable effect in this regime. Iterations 0 and 1, and 7 and 8, show the same pattern, which the critique reads as a failure set by something the controller barely touches (such as the seeded motor mismatch or start transient). No raced change has moved the oval, where progress stays near 0.16 and line_loss_events stay at 2. I have no evidence that any single further change will help, and the critique's proposed alternatives (wider span at 0.015 spacing, kp compensation) are untested. I therefore keep the raced design rather than add an unsupported variable.

Expected result: the score should reproduce about 58.17. Completion is unlikely. This race establishes a known-good fallback for the final stage, and it gives a clean baseline for the Evaluator to test.

Falsifiable criteria: oval max_error below 0.06 and line_loss_events of at most 1; progress above 0.2 on all tracks; any change in score beyond 0.01 from 58.17 would indicate run-to-run variation rather than a design effect.
